To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the vendors of 52 to 58% of the smartphone apps and 45% of the websites we investigated fulfilled our requests, (2) 20% of the websites would have provided our personal data to third parties, and (3) the vendors of smartphone apps and websites are more willing to provide data than to delete it.
(a) data subjects can obtain access to data pertaining them in about half of all cases and (b) they can demand erasures in about half of the cases.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a) the extent to which the rights of access and erasure are honoured, b) the quality of the information provided to the users, c) the extent to and ways in which personal data are disclosed to third parties, and d) the quality of data deletion.
the following questions: Do app and website owners respect the privacy of their users?
the question of whether the EU’s right of access and erasure are honoured in practice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
privacy rights have been introduced in the EU but not implemented in practice.
privacy rights are not well respected.
the privacy rights of the EU Directive 95 are not fully implemented by the service providers in our sample.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the privacy of European citizens is not sufficiently protected by law and that the enforcement of privacy rights is not sufficiently supported by technology.
privacy is still a problem in the digital world.
it is still difficult for European citizens to exert their privacy rights.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the right of access and the right to erasure are not well implemented.
the upcoming EU General Personal Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is needed.
the upcoming GDPR will not only have an effect on the vendors of apps and websites, but also on their customers.
